tells: Plain declarative build, a gloss-by-example ('A person does not try to understand their hunger; they arrive at it and feel it'), and the quotation is brought in with an attribution clause ('citing the view that'), which is how Author A does it.

'Surah Yunus adds to their names, which Sheikh Bahmanpour treats as the same people' — the relative clause hangs off 'names', not the people; Author A keeps the referent clear: 'Surah Yunus gives them a second name ... the same people'
'is still not the knowledge of those who witness it' — the hedge 'still' smooths over the contrast; Author A states the turn outright

'Imam ʿAli (as) describes what these friends see that others miss.' — ends the paragraph on a teaser for the next section; Author A ends a paragraph on its own point and lets the next paragraph take up the link

Gloss of a term in apposition ('knowledge by presence, ʿilm al-huduri'), plain short sentences, the same comma-light joining ('is another and so are pain and anxiety'), and a quoted point drawn out step by step, as the reference does with the rusted machine.

Quotations are run into the attributing sentence ('tells the traveller that he "has no right..."'), with sober reporting verbs and a restrained register, as with the Mutahhari and Khomeini quotations in the reference.

Paragraph picks up an objection and hands it to the verse ('Surah al-Nisaʾ answers that concern.'), then lays out the Sheikh's reading with glosses in brackets and semicolons; same steady expository register.
'So "ordinary people also can enter..."' — opens a paragraph with 'So' plus a bare quotation; Author A brings a quotation in with an attributing clause
'And he gives the reason it is open. We are made for it.' — 'And'-opener and staged short beat for effect; Author A would write 'He gives the reason: we are made for it'
'Hence.' — a one-word fragment as a sentence; Author A never writes fragments
'The earlier sections showed ... That is worth pursuing.' — a recap and tidy closing verdict; Author A does not sum up or end on a moral

Opens by picking up the previous rank ('Higher still is a verse about God's oneness.'), introduces the verse with a lead sentence before the block, and glosses terms in apposition ('ulu al-ʿilm', 'tawhid, God's oneness'), as Author A does.
'Then: "These are shirk."' — a staged dramatic beat with a colon and a bare quotation; Author A introduces a quotation with a full attributing clause ('he says that these are shirk')
'He ended his first lecture more strongly.' — narrates the lecture as an event, building suspense; Author A reports the Sheikh's view directly ('Sheikh Bahmanpour says...')
'Shirk, setting up a partner beside God, is the gravest charge in Islam.' — a weighty closing line to land the paragraph; Author A glosses a term in passing and does not end a paragraph on emphasis

'One addresses the heart of the seeker, the other the eye of the one choosing a guide. Neither makes powers the aim of the path.' — a balanced, aphoristic summary at the end of the paragraph with a vague 'One'/'the other'; Author A does not close on a tidy summary
'For him the feats are beside the point: something a student should look past when deciding whom to trust.' — claim, colon, restated claim; Author A states it once and plainly

'Mutahhari's words show why seeking them would be: the goal has become something other than God' — a compressed argumentative construction linking to an earlier quotation; Author A spells out the step in its own sentence

Takes up the previous paragraph ('What these people see that others miss'), explains the quotation in plain short sentences, refers back to the opening verses ('the signs of Surah al-Rum'), and uses an A-style contrast ('The Qur'an does not describe them as a theory. It describes them as believers.'), as in 'God is not withholding signs; we are failing to receive them.'

The odd comma between a long subject and its verb ('...found within the soul, must be placed there'), as in the reference's 'That something and why it is worth developing, is'; quotations are introduced by a lead sentence and then explained ('The hadith sets the two kinds of knowing side by side.').

Lead-in sentence before the quotation block, explicit callback to the prologue's opening prayer, the same comma-light joining ('as hunger is present to the one who fasts and it comes as a light'), and a measured closing that attributes its view ('in the view of Imam Khomeini and ʿAllama Tabatabaʾi').
